details:
**"The Library of Babel"**
Borges's most frequently clued story, from Ficciones. The universe is a seemingly infinite library of identical hexagonal galleries whose shelves hold every possible 410-page book made from 25 symbols (22 letters, the period, the comma, and the space). Almost all the books are gibberish. The narrator ends by guessing that the library is "unlimited and periodic," saying his "solitude is gladdened by this elegant hope."

**The Purifiers, the Crimson Hexagon, and the "Vindications"**
Details of the librarians' society in "The Library of Babel." Pilgrims hunt for "Vindications," books that would justify each person's life. Fanatical "Purifiers" destroy millions of books they think useless, and others seek the Crimson Hexagon and the "Man of the Book," a librarian said to have read the catalog of all catalogs. The story has an epigraph from Robert Burton's The Anatomy of Melancholy, and a footnote suggests the whole library could fit in a single volume with infinitely thin pages.

**"The Garden of Forking Paths," Yu Tsun, and Stephen Albert**
A World War I spy story. Dr. Yu Tsun, a Chinese professor spying for Germany in England, is pursued by Captain Richard Madden. To tell Berlin that a new British artillery park is in the French town of Albert, on the Ancre, he looks up the sinologist Stephen Albert in the phone book and murders him, knowing the newspapers will print the victim's name.

**Ts'ui Pen's labyrinth and the forbidden word "time"**
Before his death, Stephen Albert reveals that Yu Tsun's ancestor Ts'ui Pen, who retired to write a book and build a labyrinth, made them one and the same. His chaotic novel is a labyrinth in time in which every possible outcome happens at once. Albert asks, "In a riddle whose answer is chess, what is the only prohibited word?" Just as "chess" is forbidden there, the word "time" never appears in Ts'ui Pen's book, because time is its subject.

**"The Aleph" and Carlos Argentino Daneri**
The title story of a 1949 collection. After the death of his beloved Beatriz Viterbo, the narrator "Borges" keeps visiting her house and her cousin, the pompous poet Carlos Argentino Daneri. In Daneri's cellar is the Aleph, "a small iridescent sphere of almost unbearable brilliance" that contains every point in the universe seen from every angle. It is named for the first letter of the Hebrew alphabet.

**Ficciones**
Borges's most famous collection (1944). It combines The Garden of Forking Paths (1941) with a second part, Artifices, and includes "Tlön, Uqbar, Orbis Tertius," "Pierre Menard," "The Library of Babel," "Death and the Compass," "Funes the Memorious," "The South," "The Secret Miracle," and "Three Versions of Judas," in which the theologian Nils Runeberg argues that God became incarnate as Judas. Many of these stories also appear in the English selection Labyrinths.

**"Death and the Compass," Erik Lönnrot, and Red Scharlach**
A metaphysical detective story. The detective Erik Lönnrot investigates a series of murders that begins with a rabbi, beside whose typewriter is left the message "The first letter of the Name has been uttered." Lönnrot decides the killings follow the four letters of the Tetragrammaton, but the pattern is a trap set by the criminal Red Scharlach, who lures him to the villa of Triste-le-Roy and kills him. Lönnrot holds that "reality may avoid the obligation to be interesting, but... hypotheses may not."

**"Pierre Menard, Author of the Quixote"**
A story written as a mock critical essay about a fictional French Symbolist writer. Menard sets out not to copy but to compose fragments of Cervantes's Don Quixote word for word in the 20th century. The narrator argues that Menard's identical text is far richer than the original.

**"Tlön, Uqbar, Orbis Tertius"**
A story that begins when Adolfo Bioy Casares quotes a heresiarch of Uqbar: "mirrors and copulation are abominable, for they multiply the number of men." The narrator and Bioy find an article on Uqbar in only one copy of the Anglo-American Cyclopaedia, and later an encyclopedia of Tlön, an imaginary idealist world whose languages lack nouns. It turns out to be the invention of a secret society, and objects from Tlön start to appear in the real world.

**"The South" and Juan Dahlmann**
The librarian Juan Dahlmann, excited about his newly acquired copy of the Thousand and One Nights, gashes his head, nearly dies of septicemia, and then travels south to recover on his family's ranch. At a country store a drunken young tough challenges him, an old gaucho tosses him a dagger, and Dahlmann walks out onto the plain for a knife fight he is sure to lose. The ending may be his dream of a heroic death in the hospital.

**"The Lottery in Babylon"**
A narrator who has been both "proconsul" and "slave" describes how Babylon's lottery, run by the secretive Company, grew from a simple game of chance into a system in which chance governs every part of life. Losers who once had to pay fines chose jail instead, and the drawings came to hand out punishments as well as rewards.

**"The Circular Ruins"**
A story with an epigraph from Lewis Carroll's Through the Looking-Glass. A wizard comes to a ruined circular temple to dream a son into reality, building him detail by detail starting with his heart. When a fire engulfs the temple, the wizard walks into it unburned and realizes that someone else was dreaming him too.

**"The Book of Sand"**
The title story of a 1975 collection. A retired librarian trades a black-letter Wycliffe Bible for a book with infinitely many pages, labeled "Holy Writ" on its spine, from a Scottish Presbyterian Bible seller. Terrified by it, he hides it behind volumes of the Thousand and One Nights and finally loses it among the shelves of the National Library. The same collection includes "The Other," in which an old Borges meets his younger self.

**"The Zahir"**
A story from The Aleph in which the narrator "Borges" receives a twenty-centavo coin as change after a wake. The coin is the Zahir, an object that becomes impossible to forget once seen, and his obsession with it slowly crowds out everything else.

**"A Survey of the Works of Herbert Quain"**
A mock obituary and review of a fictional writer. Quain's detective novel The God of the Labyrinth deliberately offers a false solution, and his novel April March is told backward in branching chapters that combine into several different novels.
